stories.title: A junction with a shorter address
stories.transcript:
Tally Ho Corner grew out of two roads meeting. Ballards Lane was a medieval road, but for centuries it stopped short of the High Road. The connection came in 1756, when the lane was extended to join what was then the Great North Road. North Finchley had become a junction on the road out of London.

In the following century, a new toll road from Marylebone joined this route through Ballards Lane. Long-distance travellers needed more than a road: their coaches needed fresh horses. Barnet's local history records sixteen horses kept near this corner by the Tally Ho Coach Company, ready for the Birmingham coach's first change.

That gives Tally Ho a coaching connection. But a Victorian cyclist offered a different account of the name, involving a friend with a postcard to write.

Writing in 1880 as Le Voyageur, he described meeting that friend here for bicycle rides. They came by different roads, so this was a convenient rendezvous. Describing it every time was less convenient. His friend grew tired of writing “Junction of North and Finchley roads” and came up with Tally Ho Corner instead.

According to the writer, cycling notices spread the name, and a local hotel put it above the door. His account doesn't settle who used it first. But it's a pleasingly practical contribution to local history: two people arranging a bicycle ride, and one of them deciding that their meeting place needed a shorter address.

When you are ready, follow the Ballards Lane pavement south, back towards artsdepot. Grand Arcade is about seventy-five metres away, before Nether Street. Stop at its street entrance.

stories.title: Guitar strings in the Grand Arcade
stories.transcript:
The Grand Arcade belongs to the North Finchley of the 1930s: a covered shopping passage, with a name that promises a little more ceremony than an ordinary row of shops. Its Art Deco design gave everyday errands a setting of their own, tucked away from the main street.

One of those errands was buying guitar strings. Dave Davies, who grew up in Muswell Hill and became the Kinks’ guitarist, remembered coming to the arcade’s music shop as a teenager. Before a guitar becomes part of a famous band’s sound, it still needs the small, unglamorous things a shop can supply.

Years later, Davies supported a campaign to secure recognition for the arcade. Local campaigner Ian Dunn helped lead that effort, and in 2022 the arcade was added to Barnet’s local heritage list. That recognition recorded the value people placed on a building woven into their ordinary lives.

There is something appealing about that kind of attachment. A grand name gets you through the entrance; buying something small, returning for it, and remembering the shopkeeper can make a place your own.

For the next story, return north along Ballards Lane towards Tally Ho, then continue along the High Road to Lodge Lane. The former Torrington pub stood at that corner, historically number 811 High Road. Use the pedestrian crossings where needed and stop clear of the junction.

stories.title: Eighty pence at the Torrington
stories.transcript:
This corner once had its own live-music address: the Torrington pub, at Lodge Lane and the High Road. It was rebuilt in 1962 and closed in 2004. A concert advertisement preserved by the local history society gives us a much closer view than those dates do.

In June 1977, the bill advertised John Otway and Wild Willy Barrett for a Sunday night. Doors opened at a quarter past eight, and admission was eighty pence. The following Sunday had another act on the bill. This was a place where live music could be a regular part of the week.

Picture the scale of a pub gig: instruments close enough to see hands working, glasses being set down, conversations overlapping while the musicians get ready. Then the first amplified notes change the room. The people who came in separately become, for a while, an audience. That is an imagined scene, but the modest Sunday-night advertisement gives it a very ordinary, local footing.

The Torrington’s story is often told through the names of musicians associated with it. This little advert offers another way in: an address nearby, a start time, and the possibility of hearing something live before Monday came round. For the price of admission, an ordinary evening could acquire a soundtrack.

Now retrace the High Road south towards Tally Ho and continue along Ballards Lane. Turn into Nether Street beside artsdepot, away from the main road. Trinity Church is a short walk along Nether Street.

stories.title: The work behind the concert
stories.transcript:
Trinity Church is also a place where an orchestra gets its music ready. Finchley Symphony Orchestra uses it for rehearsals and concerts. The players are non-professional, but their repertoire is ambitious, reaching from Beethoven to less familiar composers such as Leokadiya Kashperova.

Their own account of rehearsal life makes room for something less grand: tea, cake and a chat. There is a weekly rhythm to this kind of music-making, with the social break sitting comfortably beside the difficult score.

We can picture a rehearsal rather than a performance: a phrase tried again, a pencil lifted to mark the page, a player waiting while another section works through its part. Gradually, separate efforts begin to fit together. None of that requires a concert audience, though it is what eventually makes the concert possible.

From the pavement, the building keeps that weekly work to itself. It is a useful addition to the street’s soundscape, even on a day when all we hear here is passing traffic.

For the final story, follow Nether Street back towards Ballards Lane and artsdepot. Stop outside the arts centre, clear of the bus station access.

stories.title: An audience at Tally Ho
stories.transcript:
Before artsdepot, this part of Tally Ho had a Gaumont cinema. It opened in 1937, with a rounded brick tower and a large carved panel showing a film being made: actors, a director, lights and a camera. The building advertised the magic of cinema by showing some of the work behind it.

Picture an evening there: the street left behind, rows of seats spreading out beneath an elaborate ceiling, warm wooden panelling along the lower walls. Conversation drifts across the auditorium. Then the lights fall, the screen brightens, and everyone’s attention turns in the same direction. A journey to somewhere else begins a short walk from home.

The cinema closed in 1980 and was demolished in 1987. But the later arts centre was something local people actively asked for. artsdepot traces its beginnings to a 1996 community conference where residents called for a place for the arts. Public meetings and council backing helped turn that request into a project that could be built.

It took persistence. When a proposal emerged to turn the planned venue into a library, campaigners protested. The centre’s own history recalls masks, banners and a performance by Madness at the rally. The arts plan survived, and artsdepot opened in 2004.

It is an apt place to finish: at a venue that needed its audience before it could open its doors. People first had to make the case for having it here. The performances could follow.

This is the end of the walk, back by North Finchley bus station. Choose End tour to stop location tracking. There is no need to enter the arts centre.
